item.title: Trump defiant after voters deliver verdict. Live updates here.
item.description: Amid a churning trade dispute, the Trump administration faces a major test. What does it mean for Canada? Follow for live updates.
item.dc:creator: CTVNews.ca Staff
item.content:encoded: In a sweeping upset to U.S. President Donald Trump’s power in Washington, the Democrats have retaken control of the American legislative branch. Democrats won control of the Senate and Congress, in a widespread rebuke of Trump and the Republican Party, The Associated Press reported. Two years deep into a trade war, Canadians wait to see the impacts of the shift in the balance of power, but on Wednesday it remained unclear how the results will impact trade negotiations. The two sides have yet to come to an agreement, and while Prime Minister Mark Carney indicated progress, political watchers say immediate relief is unlikely. item.title: U.S. futures sharply higher after Democratic route in midterm elections
item.description: U.S. stock futures surged Wednesday after the U.S. midterm election yielded Democratic majorities in both houses of Congress. Investors parsed the potential impact on artificial intelligence, the ...
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: NEW YORK — U.S. stocks are surging Wednesday after U.S. President Donald Trump’s party lost its sole control of Washington in the midterm elections. Stocks generally do well in the months following any midterm U.S. election, regardless of who wins, and the S&P 500 soared 1.8 per cent toward its best day in three months. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 1,112 points, or 2.1 per cent, as of 10 a.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 2.4 per cent higher. Stocks of solar-power companies helped lead the way as Wall Street tried to sort the winners and losers from the widespread losses for Republicans. Investors, meanwhile, see risks ahead for Trump’s social-media company, the artificial-intelligence industry and businesses owned by Elon Musk, who donated heavily to Republicans. Strategists along Wall Street had been urging investors not to get swept up in the election because it may not matter much for the broad market in the long term. Prices for stocks depend more on where profits for companies and interest rates are heading than on who controls what in Washington. “Earnings trump elections,” according to Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management. Still, Wall Street may have gotten a preferred political scenario as Democrats are set to take control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives. That could counterbalance Trump’s White House, and Wall Street generally prefers split control of Washington because it lessens the risk of transformative changes to the economy. Much remains impossible to predict, of course, and Trump retains executive authority over key areas such as defense, foreign policy and in some instances trade. A downbeat forecast could be that “Trump is not now a lame duck, but an angry duck” who might restart tensions over tariffs and NATO allies’ levels of military spending, said Carsten Brzeski, global chief of macro at ING Bank. An optimistic view, Brzeski said, is that Trump becomes “a tame duck ... that he will slow down any disruptive efforts and that he will put more focus on trying to win the Nobel Peace Prize by ending the two big wars without big disruption, and on trade, nothing happens but a few words.” Here’s a look at some of the moves rippling through financial markets: Trump Media and Tesla are down Trump’s social-media company, Trump Media & Technology Group, was one of the market’s bigger losers following the election and dropped 9.5 per cent. It had already come into the day with a loss of 55.1 per cent for the year so far as Trump’s approval ratings had weakened. Since briefly touching a peak of US$175 five years ago, it’s dropped toward US$5. Its main business is Truth Social, which is most well known for Trump’s postings on the platform. Elon Musk’s businesses also struggled. Tesla fell 3.6 per cent, and SpaceX sank 3 per cent. Musk, a former top Trump adviser, is among the possible targets for investigations by a Democratic-controlled Congress. AI companies in general are under pressure Trump has been a big backer of the AI industry, and Democratic control of Capitol Hill could mean more regulation or restrictions for the industry. Concerns have grown across political parties about AI in general. Investors see Democratic victories in Texas in particular as possibly slowing the buildout of further AI data centers. Nvidia, the chip company that quickly became the poster child of the frenzy around AI-related stocks, slipped 0.5 per cent after falling as much as 2.8 per cent earlier in the morning. CoreWeave, a company that rents out access to AI chips to customers over the loud, fell 6.8 per cent Advanced Micro Devices, another chip giant, held up better. It rose 3.4 per cent after reporting much stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Green power companies are up Democratic control of Congress could light the way for companies in the solar and wind industries. First Solar jumped 11.1 per cent, and Enphase Energy climbed 11.6 per cent. Bond yields are down In the bond market, Treasury yields eased. That could be a signal that investors see less risk of Washington piling even more debt onto its already big mountain. Treasury yields had surged through the summer and reached their highest levels in decades because of worries about the U.S. government’s big debt, along with higher inflation and other concerns. A Congress controlled by Democrats could provide a check against more spending and cuts to taxes that would widen Washington’s deficit. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.92 per cent from 4.95 per cent late Tuesday. Stocks rally in much of the world Indexes climbed across most of the world. Stocks jumped 2.2 per cent in Paris, 2.2 per cent in Shanghai and 1.8 per cent in London. Japan’s Nikkei 225 was an outlier and fell 1.4 per cent. Stocks worldwide got a boost from easing oil prices. Brent crude, the international standard, dropped 2.9 per cent to US$100.63 amid continued uncertainty about what the war with Iran will mean for the global energy industry. The price for the most actively traded contract in the Brent market has been veering between roughly US$70 and US$120 per barrel since just before the war with Iran began. ___ Stan Choe and David Mchugh, The Associated Press AP Writer Elaine Lai contributed to this report from Hong Kong, and McHugh contributed from Frankfurt, Germany.

item.title: S&P/TSX composite up nearly 500 points after Democrats take control of U.S. Congress
item.description: Canada’s main stock index jumped nearly 500 points, while U.S. stock markets also shot higher in early trading after midterm elections in the United States.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — Canada’s main stock index jumped nearly 500 points, while U.S. stock markets also shot higher in early trading after midterm elections in the United States saw the Democrats take control in both houses of Congress. The S&P/TSX composite index was up 480.11 points at 36,012.39. In New York, the Dow Jones industrial average was up 1,173.36 points at 52,960.08. The S&P 500 index was up 102.23 points at 7,671.15, while the Nasdaq composite was up 310.72 points at 25,682.73. The Canadian dollar traded for 71.68 cents US compared with 71.46 cents US on Tuesday. The December crude oil contract was down US$3.11 at US$92.98 per barrel. The December gold contract was up US$107.40 at US$4,047.80 an ounce. --- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

item.title: StatCan reports $5.4B merchandise trade surplus for September
item.description: Statistics Canada says the country’s merchandise trade surplus increased to $5.4 billion in September as exports edged higher and imports decreased.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: OTTAWA — Statistics Canada says the country’s merchandise trade surplus increased to $5.4 billion in September as exports edged higher and imports decreased. The agency says the result compared with a trade surplus of $5 billion in August. Total exports edged up 0.2 per cent in September to $78.6 billion, boosted by exports of crude oil and gold. Exports of energy products rose 8.2 per cent in September, helped by higher oil prices, while exports of metal and non-metallic mineral products, which includes unwrought gold, increased 8.6 per cent. Total imports fell 0.3 per cent in September to $73.2 billion as imports of motor vehicles and parts fell 9.1 per cent in the month. In volume terms, total exports fell four per cent, while imports fell 2.5 per cent. --- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.
